claim: DopaFilm is a 2D composite nanofilm engineered from oligonucleotide-functionalized single-wall carbon nanotubes assembled in solution phase.
source: To address this, we engineered a chemi-sensitive, two-dimensional composite nanofilm that facilitates visualization of the release and diffusion of the neurochemical dopamine with synaptic resolution, quantal sensitivity, and simultaneously from hundreds of release sites.
evidence: The manuscript describes the engineering of the nanofilm and its composition in the methods section.

claim: DopaFilm facilitates visualization of dopamine release and diffusion with synaptic resolution and quantal sensitivity.
source: To address this, we engineered a chemi-sensitive, two-dimensional composite nanofilm that facilitates visualization of the release and diffusion of the neurochemical dopamine with synaptic resolution, quantal sensitivity, and simultaneously from hundreds of release sites.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the capabilities of DopaFilm.

claim: Dopamine release is broadcast from a subset of dendritic processes as hotspots with a mean spatial spread of approximately 3.2 µm (FWHM).
source: We found that dopamine release is broadcast from a subset of dendritic processes as hotspots that have a mean spatial spread of ≈ 3.2 µm (full width at half maximum [FWHM]) and are observed with a mean spatial frequency of one hotspot per ≈ 7.5 µm of dendritic length.
evidence: The abstract provides quantitative measurements of spatial spread.

claim: Dopamine release hotspots are observed with a mean spatial frequency of one hotspot per approximately 7.5 µm of dendritic length.
source: We found that dopamine release is broadcast from a subset of dendritic processes as hotspots that have a mean spatial spread of ≈ 3.2 µm (full width at half maximum [FWHM]) and are observed with a mean spatial frequency of one hotspot per ≈ 7.5 µm of dendritic length.
evidence: The abstract provides quantitative measurements of spatial frequency.

claim: Major dendrites, fine dendritic processes, and dendritic arbors of dopamine neurons participate in dopamine release.
source: Major dendrites of dopamine neurons and fine dendritic processes, as well as dendritic arbors and dendrites with no apparent varicose morphology participated in dopamine release.
evidence: The abstract explicitly lists the types of dendritic structures involved in release.

claim: Dopamine release hotspots co-localize with Bassoon.
source: Remarkably, these release hotspots co-localized with Bassoon, suggesting that Bassoon may contribute to organizing active zones in dendrites, similar to its role in axon terminals.
evidence: The abstract states the co-localization finding.

claim: Bassoon may contribute to organizing active zones in dendrites, similar to its role in axon terminals.
source: Remarkably, these release hotspots co-localized with Bassoon, suggesting that Bassoon may contribute to organizing active zones in dendrites, similar to its role in axon terminals.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a suggestion based on the co-localization data.

claim: Chemical neurotransmission is one of the fundamental modalities of communication between neurons.
source: Chemical neurotransmission constitutes one of the fundamental modalities of communication between neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: Fast synaptic transmission primarily employs glutamate or γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA).
source: Synapses that mediate rapid communication between most excitatory and inhibitory synapses in the brain primarily employ glutamate or γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Fast synaptic transmission occurs at highly specialized synaptic structures with nanoscale spatial organization and millisecond temporal precision.
source: Such chemical communication occurs at highly specialized synaptic structures that have nanoscale spatial organization and operate with millisecond temporal precision (Clements et al., 1992; Südhof, 2012; Choquet and Triller, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neuromodulators operate at different spatiotemporal scales than fast synaptic transmitters.
source: In contrast, neuromodulators, including biogenic amines, neuropeptides, and hormones, operate at different spatiotemporal scales.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Neuromodulatory synapses do not exhibit close apposition to their partners but act on extrasynaptically localized receptors.
source: Neuromodulatory synapses do not exhibit a close apposition to their partners but act on receptors that are extrasynaptically localized, and signal through G-protein coupled intracellular mechanisms (Greengard, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Neuromodulators diffuse from their release sites in adequate quantities to influence target receptors.
source: This suggests that neuromodulators diffuse from their release sites in adequate quantities to influence target receptors (Agnati et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons are known for their large size and exhibit highly ramified axonal arborizations and dense varicosities.
source: Dopaminergic neurons are known for their large size and exhibit highly ramified axonal arborizations and dense varicosities (Matsuda et al., 2009; Pacelli et al., 2015; Bolam and Pissadaki, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Previous studies have not measured dopamine efflux with single release site resolution.
source: Studies have sought to establish the molecular determinants of dopamine release from these dense axonal arbors, but these attempts do not rely on measurement of dopamine efflux with single release site resolution (Ducrot et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dopamine neurons possess the machinery for co-release of other neurotransmitters, including glutamate and GABA.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that dopamine neurons possess the machinery for co-release of other neurotransmitters, including glutamate and GABA, but to what extent, if any, co-release events spatially overlap remains insufficiently understood (Stuber et al., 2010; Sulzer et al., 1998; Tritsch et al., 2016; Tritsch et al., 2012; Fortin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Somatodendritic release of dopamine constitutes an important component of dopamine signaling.
source: Electrochemical and microdialysis assays in midbrain regions have shown that somatodendritic release of dopamine constitutes an important component of dopamine signaling, with notable implications in disease and behavior (Beckstead et al., 2004; Gantz et al., 2013; Björklund and Lindvall, 1975; Cheramy et al., 1981; Cragg et al., 1997; Ludwig et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The spatial and temporal dynamics of dendritic release events and their regulatory mechanisms remain poorly characterized.
source: However, the spatial and temporal dynamics of dendritic release events and their regulatory mechanisms remain poorly characterized.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge in the introduction.

claim: DopaFilm was fabricated by drop-casting glass coverslips with dopamine nanosensors to produce a 2D layer of turn-on fluorescent, dopamine-sensitive surface.
source: In this study, we drop-cast glass coverslips with dopamine nanosensors to produce a 2D layer of a turn-on fluorescent, dopamine-sensitive surface that can effectively image dopamine diffusion from a point source (Figure 1A).
evidence: The methods section describes the fabrication process.

claim: DopaFilm sensors exhibit subsecond turn-on responses.
source: Temporally, the sensors exhibit subsecond turn-on responses, which enabled real-time imaging of dopamine's temporal evolution.
evidence: The results section describes the temporal properties of the sensors.

claim: About 79% of TH-GFP+ neurons were confirmed to be dopaminergic in retrospective immunofluorescence against TH.
source: About 79% of TH-GFP+ neurons were confirmed to be dopaminergic in retrospective immunofluorescence against TH, the rate-limiting enzyme in dopamine biosynthesis.
evidence: The results section provides this quantitative validation.

claim: All TH-immunoreactive neurons expressed the virally delivered TH-GFP transgene.
source: On the other hand, all of the TH-immunoreactive neurons expressed the virally delivered TH-GFP transgene.
evidence: The results section provides this validation.

claim: Fluorescence hotspots in axonal arbors co-localized with TH+ boutons.
source: Whenever targeted to TH+ neurons (further confirmed by retrospective immunofluorescence experiments), our stimulation protocol elicited robust fluorescence transients from DopaFilm (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—animation 1), and the fluorescence hotspots co-localized with TH+ boutons in axonal arbors (Figure 2C).
evidence: The results section describes co-localization with reference to figures.

claim: Diffusive broadening of fluorescence hotspots was observed in subsequent imaging frames.
source: We observed diffusive broadening of the fluorescence hotspots in subsequent imaging frames (Figure 2A, +1 s), and fluorescence transients returned to baseline in the poststimulation epoch (Figure 2A post, Figure 2B).
evidence: The results section describes temporal dynamics with reference to figures.

claim: The estimated mass diffusivities from DopaFilm hotspots are approximately 1.1 ± 0.8 × 10–6 cm2 s–1.
source: The observed spatiotemporal evolution of DopaFilm hotspots is consistent with that of release and diffusion from multiple point-like sources localized in a 2D plane, with estimated mass diffusivities of ≈ 1.1 ± 0.8 × 10–6 cm2 s–1 (mean ± SD), in reasonable agreement with estimated values of diffusion coefficient for dopamine (Cragg et al., 2001).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative measurements and comparison to literature.

claim: Fluorescence transients were observed to emanate from a subset of varicosities while another subset produced no corresponding fluorescence hotspots.
source: Despite the high density of axonal varicosities in the FOV, fluorescence transients were observed to emanate from a subset of varicosities while another subset of varicosities produced no corresponding ∆F/F fluorescence hotspots (Figure 2C, red arrows).
evidence: The results section describes heterogeneity in release with reference to figures.

claim: The percentage of release-competent boutons varied greatly in axonal arbors, ranging from 5% to 65%, with a mean of 32%.
source: The percentage of release-competent boutons varied greatly in axonal arbors, ranging from 5% in some FOVs to 65% in others, with a mean of 32% of putative boutons participating in release.
evidence: The results section provides quantitative measurements of release-competent boutons.

claim: The sparse-release observation is in agreement with results from previous studies.
source: This sparse-release observation is in agreement with results from previous studies (Liu et al., 2018; Pereira et al., 2016).
evidence: The results section compares findings to prior work.

claim: The turn-on kinetics (τpeak) of measured transients in axons were 0.46 ± 0.16 s (mean ± SD).
source: The turn-on and clearance kinetics of the measured transients in axons were 0.46 ± 0.16 s (mean ± SD) for time to peak (τpeak) and 3.83 ± 0.8 s (mean ± SD) for first-order decay time constant (τoff) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative kinetic measurements.

claim: The clearance kinetics (τoff) of measured transients in axons were 3.83 ± 0.8 s (mean ± SD).
source: The turn-on and clearance kinetics of the measured transients in axons were 0.46 ± 0.16 s (mean ± SD) for time to peak (τpeak) and 3.83 ± 0.8 s (mean ± SD) for first-order decay time constant (τoff) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative kinetic measurements.

claim: The turn-on kinetics of DopaFilm is slower than those reported for GRABDA and dLight.
source: The turn-on kinetics is slower than those reported for the genetically encoded dopamine sensors GRABDA (≈ 100 ms) and dLight (reported as τ1/2 of ≈10 ms followed by a plateau of ≈100 ms) (Patriarchi et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: The results section compares kinetics to other sensors with citations.

claim: Decay kinetics of DopaFilm appears to be slower than dLight and comparable to or faster than GRABDA.
source: On the other hand, decay kinetics appears to be slower than dLight (reported as τ1/2 ≈ 100 ms) and comparable to or faster than those reported for GRABDA (≈ 3–17 s for variants).
evidence: The results section compares kinetics to other sensors.

claim: Stimulation of ChrimsonR+ in TH− neurons did not elicit fluorescence transients in DopaFilm.
source: The DopaFilm was responsive only to the activity of TH+ neurons. Stimulation of ChrimsonR+ in TH− neurons did not elicit fluorescence transients in DopaFilm, and neither evoked nor spontaneous activities were noted in neurons that lacked TH immunoreactivity despite being TH-GFP+ in the viral expression paradigm (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section describes control experiments.

claim: Both evoked and spontaneous DopaFilm fluorescence transients were absent when imaging in extracellular Ca2+-free media.
source: Both evoked and spontaneous DopaFilm fluorescence transients were absent when imaging in extracellular 'Ca2+-free' media (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The results section describes control experiments.

claim: Repeat stimulations can be carried out with rest periods of approximately 2–3 min between stimuli, giving rise to a consistent set of DopaFilm hotspot activities.
source: In axon terminals, we observed that repeat stimulations can be carried out with rest periods of ~ 2–3 min between stimuli, giving rise to a consistent set of DopaFilm hotspot activities, and suggesting that release-competent dopamine neuron boutons likely have a high probability of release (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: The results section describes reproducibility experiments.

claim: Hotspot centroids were remarkably consistent across repeat stimulations.
source: We found that hotspot centroids were remarkably consistent across repeat stimulations (Figure 3C).
evidence: The results section describes spatial consistency with reference to figures.

claim: DopaFilm hotspot centroids and bouton centroids matched with remarkable consistency across stimuli (no offset in some ROIs, <5 camera pixels for all ROIs, equivalent to <1.7 µm).
source: Our results showed that ∆F/F hotspot centroids and bouton centroids matched with remarkable consistency across stimuli (no offset in some regions of interest [ROIs], <5 camera pixels for all ROIs, equivalent to <1.7 µm; Figure 3E).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative spatial measurements.

claim: DopaFilm activity hotspots can be faithfully localized to the same set of boutons across stimulation epochs.
source: These experiments demonstrate that DopaFilm activity hotspots can be faithfully localized to the same set of boutons across stimulation epochs and are therefore likely driven by the efflux of dopamine from putative active zones of these boutons.
evidence: The results section draws conclusions from the consistency data.

claim: Application of nomifensine altered the clearance kinetics of DopaFilm transients.
source: Application of NOM altered the clearance kinetics of DopaFilm transients, defined by a first-order decay time constant, τoff (mean ± SD of τoff for artificial cerebrospinal fluid [ACSF]: 4.38 ± 0.84 and for +NOM: 5.70 ± 1.47, p-value=3×10–4, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and dramatically affected the overall kinetic profile of ∆F/F traces, indicated by mean FWHM of 1.85 s before and 4.45 s after application of NOM (Figure 3F–J).
evidence: The results section describes pharmacological manipulation experiments.

claim: The measured peak amplitude of the ∆F/F trace was higher after application of nomifensine (mean peak ∆F/F = 15.7% before and 24.5% after).
source: Additionally, the measured peak amplitude of the ∆F/F trace was higher after application of NOM (mean peak ∆F/F = 15.7% before and 24.5% after application of NOM; Figure 3F–J).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative measurements of drug effects.

claim: Application of nomifensine did not reveal any subthreshold activity at silent varicosities.
source: Importantly, application of NOM did not reveal any subthreshold activity at silent varicosities that could have gone undetected in pre-NOM imaging sessions (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: The results section describes negative findings from drug experiments.

claim: The absence of DopaFilm fluorescence transient is likely an indication of a lack of dopamine release at release-incompetent varicosities.
source: Thus, we conclude that DopaFilm hotspot activity arises from dopamine release at varicosities, and that the absence of DopaFilm fluorescence transient is likely an indication of a lack of dopamine release at release-incompetent varicosities.
evidence: The results section draws conclusions from the nomifensine experiments.

claim: Application of NBQX abolished spontaneous DopaFilm activities that were detected before application.
source: We imaged from these neurons under ACSF (our normal imaging buffer) and then bath-applied NBQX (10 µM). DopaFilm activities that were detected before application of NBQX were absent in the postdrug imaging sessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B).
evidence: The results section describes pharmacological manipulation experiments.

claim: Combined application of NBQX and D-AP5 resulted in reduced dopamine release as measured by peak amplitude and area under the curve of ∆F/F traces.
source: Here, such treatment resulted in reduced dopamine release as measured by the peak amplitude of ∆F/F traces and the area under the curve of ∆F/F traces (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-E).
evidence: The results section describes pharmacological manipulation experiments.

claim: DopaFilm can detect 1 nM concentrations of dopamine in bath application experiments.
source: In in vitro experiments, we determined that DopaFilm exhibits high sensitivity to dopamine and can detect 1 nM concentrations in bath application experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The results section provides sensitivity measurements.

claim: DopaFilm has an apparent dissociation constant (Kd) of 268 nM.
source: Dopamine wash experiments revealed DopaFilm has the sensitivity to detect 1 nM concentrations, remained stable over the duration of a typical experiment, and has an apparent dissociation constant (Kd) of 268 nM (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-C).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative binding measurements.

claim: Bath application of TTX abolished synchronous, evoked release of dopamine but stochastic, temporally uncorrelated fluorescence transients persisted.
source: As expected, bath application of 10 µM TTX abolished synchronous, evoked release of dopamine but stochastic, temporally uncorrelated fluorescence transients, which we refer to as spontaneous release events, persisted (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—animation 1 before TTX, Figure 4—animation 2 after TTX).
evidence: The results section describes TTX experiments.

claim: The spatial extent of DopaFilm fluorescence hotspots was diminished after application of TTX.
source: The spatial extent of DopaFilm fluorescence hotspots was diminished after application of TTX (Figure 4A, B and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and the peak amplitude of transients was smaller compared to evoked release (Figure 4E).
evidence: The results section describes TTX effects on spatial properties.

claim: TTX transients occurred with a frequency of 0.29 ± 0.24 s–1 per release site (mean ± SD).
source: Interestingly, we observed that TTX transients occurred with a frequency of (mean ± SD) 0.29 ± 0.24 s–1 per release site, which contrasted with a frequency of (mean ± SD) 0.16 ± 0.13 s–1 per release site for spontaneous activities before TTX addition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H-I).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative frequency measurements.

claim: DopaFilm fluorescence transients in TTX were detected with a robust SNR of more than 5.
source: Notably, DopaFilm fluorescence transients in TTX were still detected with a robust SNR of more than 5, where the SNR is defined as the ratio of ∆F to the SD of F0 (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative SNR measurements.

claim: A three-component Gaussian mixture model (GMM) with mean parameters µ1=5.7%, µ2=9.6%, and µ3=15.1% ∆F/F offered the best fit for TTX transient data.
source: We found that a three-component GMM whose mean parameters (µ) are µ1=5.7%, µ2=9.6%, and µ3=15.1% ∆F/F offered the best fit (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The results section describes statistical modeling of the data.

claim: DopaFilm transients that are measured in TTX represent quantal release events of dopamine.
source: In summary, our experimental results and statistical analysis demonstrate that DopaFilm transients that are measured in TTX represent quantal release events of dopamine and, to our knowledge, offer the only experimental observation of putative single-vesicle fusion events in which the released neurochemical can be visualized in both spatial and temporal domains.
evidence: The results section draws conclusions from TTX and statistical modeling experiments.

claim: DopaFilm detected both evoked and spontaneous transients that clearly emanated from MAP2+ and TH+ dendritic processes of dopamine neurons.
source: When deployed for imaging activity in somatodendritic compartments of dopamine neurons, DopaFilm detected both evoked and spontaneous transients that clearly emanated from MAP2+ and TH+ dendritic processes of dopamine neurons (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section describes dendritic imaging experiments.

claim: DopaFilm transients were observed at dendritic varicosities and dendritic processes that did not appear to have any varicose morphology.
source: DopaFilm transients were observed at dendritic varicosities (i.e. bouton-like structures on dendrites; Figure 5B) and dendritic processes that did not appear to have any varicose morphology (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The results section describes morphological diversity of release sites.

claim: The spatial spread of dopamine from a dendritic release site was approximately 3.2 µm ± 3 µm (mean ± SD).
source: We computed the FWHM of each hotspot as a proxy to estimate the spatial spread of dopamine from a dendritic release site and obtained values of ≈ 3.2 µm ±3 µm (mean ± SD).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative spatial measurements.

claim: In axons, spatial spreads of approximately 6.6 µm ± 3.6 µm (mean ± SD) were observed.
source: In axons, we observed spatial spreads of ≈ 6.6 µm ± 3.6 µm (mean ± SD) (Figure 5—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative spatial measurements for comparison.

claim: Dendritic hotspots were encountered at a frequency of approximately 7.5 µm ± 0.7 µm (mean ± SD) along active dendrites.
source: Dendritic hotspots were encountered at a frequency of ≈ 7.5 µm ± 0.7 µm (mean ± SD) along the active dendrites which participated in release (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative spatial frequency measurements.

claim: Dendritic release is fast and Ca2+ dependent.
source: Our results show that dopamine neurons can sustain robust levels of release from their dendritic processes. Indeed, we demonstrate that dendritic release is fast and Ca2+ dependent, suggesting gating of dopamine release by a Ca2+-mediated release machinery, reminiscent of classical active zones.
evidence: The abstract summarizes findings about dendritic release properties.

claim: Little direct activity arose from soma of dopamine neurons.
source: As was often the case in most imaging sessions, we saw little direct activity arising from soma of dopamine neurons (Figure 5A).
evidence: The results section describes observations about somatic release.

claim: DopaFilm activity can be observed on the major dendrites of dopamine neurons, including at the junction between the soma and dendrite.
source: First, we noticed that DopaFilm activity can often be observed on the major dendrites of dopamine neurons (i.e. the stereotypic thick dendritic trunks that depart from the soma), including at the junction between the soma and dendrite (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section describes spatial patterns of release.

claim: Bassoon was enriched at dendritic locations where DopaFilm ∆F/F hotspot activity was observed.
source: These experiments showed that Bassoon was enriched at dendritic locations where we observe DopaFilm ∆F/F hotspot activity (Figure 6, Figure 5—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: The results section describes co-localization experiments.

claim: Density of Bassoon expression at a location correlated positively with the magnitude of ∆F/F activity measured by DopaFilm at the same location.
source: Importantly, density of Bassoon expression at a location correlated positively with the magnitude of ∆F/F activity measured by DopaFilm at the same location (Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: The results section describes quantitative correlation analysis.

claim: Bassoon likely plays a key role in organizing dendritic release of dopamine in a manner reminiscent of its function in nerve terminals.
source: These results suggest that Bassoon likely plays a key role in organizing dendritic release of dopamine in a manner that is reminiscent of its function in nerve terminals.
evidence: The results section draws conclusions from Bassoon co-localization data.

claim: DopaFilm activity along a dendritic process exhibited a strong correlation with the expression level of synaptobrevin-2.
source: When imaging in dendritic arbors, we observed that DopaFilm activity along a dendritic process exhibited a strong correlation with the expression level of synaptobrevin-2, while TH+ segments with no synaptobrevin-2 expression lacked a corresponding DopaFilm activity (Figure 7).
evidence: The results section describes correlation with synaptobrevin-2.

claim: DopaFilm inherently covers a large 2D plane and is capable of detecting chemical efflux at the source and tracking the signal to the end of its spatial extent.
source: DopaFilm inherently covers a large 2D plane and is therefore capable of detecting chemical efflux at the source (synapse) and tracks the signal to the end of its inherent spatial extent, subject to its limit of detection.
evidence: The discussion describes the design advantages of DopaFilm.

claim: Somatodendritic release of dopamine arises primarily from the dendrites and not the soma.
source: Our results show that somatodendritic release of dopamine arises primarily from the dendrites and not the soma.
evidence: The discussion summarizes findings about dendritic vs somatic release.

claim: Dendritic hotspots appeared localized in their spatial extent to the immediate vicinity of the release site in contrast to release in axonal processes.
source: Dendritic activity shared much in common with dynamics observed in axons, but dendritic hotspots appeared localized in their spatial extent to the immediate vicinity of the release site in contrast to release in axonal processes, which propagated to a larger spatial extent.
evidence: The discussion compares dendritic and axonal release properties.

claim: Dendritic release was observed to be robust, Ca2+-dependent, and is broadcast from hotspots that are enriched with the presynaptic active zone protein Bassoon.
source: Dendritic release was observed to be robust, Ca2+-dependent, and is broadcast from hotspots that are enriched with the presynaptic active zone protein Bassoon.
evidence: The discussion summarizes key findings about dendritic release.

claim: This study ascribes an important role for the SNARE-complex protein synaptobrevin-2 in dendritic dopamine release.
source: Our study ascribes an important role for the SNARE-complex protein synaptobrevin-2 in dendritic dopamine release, consistent with predications from previous studies (Witkovsky et al., 2009).
evidence: The discussion summarizes findings about synaptobrevin-2 with citation.

claim: Most genetically encoded biosensors for neurochemicals are primarily optimized for large-scale multicellular imaging or fiber photometry experiments.
source: Most genetically encoded biosensors for neurochemicals are primarily optimized for large-scale multicellular imaging or fiber photometry experiments (Patriarchi et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018; Marvin et al., 2013).
evidence: The discussion compares DopaFilm to other technologies with citations.

claim: DopaFilm's non-photobleaching fluorescence in the NIR to SWIR regions is spectrally compatible with existing optical technologies.
source: Moreover, DopaFilm's non-photobleaching fluorescence in the NIR to SWIR regions of the electromagnetic spectrum (0.85–1.35 µm) is spectrally compatible with existing optical technologies, as we have demonstrated in this study.
evidence: The discussion describes spectral properties of DopaFilm.

claim: DopaFilm requires use of detectors with InGaAs sensors for photon detection.
source: DopaFilm requires use of detectors with InGaAs sensors for photon detection and additional optimization of optical components to facilitate transmission of NIR and SWIR photons.
evidence: The discussion describes technical requirements for using DopaFilm.

claim: The electrophysiological properties of hippocampal neurons grown on DopaFilm were similar to neurons grown on sensor-free substrates.
source: The electrophysiological properties of hippocampal neurons grown on DopaFilm were similar to neurons that were grown on sensor-free substrates, which suggested that the electrophysiological phenotype of neurons grown DopaFilm was not altered (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section describes validation experiments.

claim: DopaFilm fluoresced in the NIR to SWIR regions of the spectrum (850–1350 nm) when imaged with a 785 nm excitation laser.
source: DopaFilm fluoresced in the NIR to short-wave infrared (SWIR) regions of the spectrum (850–1350 nm) when imaged with a 785 nm excitation laser, permitting its multiplexed deployment with existing optical technologies with no spectral overlap (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The results section describes spectral properties.

claim: DopaFilm remained stable over the duration of a typical experiment (35 days).
source: Dopamine wash experiments revealed DopaFilm has the sensitivity to detect 1 nM concentrations, remained stable over the duration of a typical experiment, and has an apparent dissociation constant (Kd) of 268 nM (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-C).
evidence: The results section describes stability measurements.

claim: The apparent Kd of DopaFilm (268 nM) is within the range of physiologically relevant concentrations for dopamine receptors.
source: This compares to half maximal effective concentrations(EC50 )values of ~ 1 µM for D1-like and ~ 10 nM for D2-like dopamine receptors, suggesting that DopaFilm is sensitive to chemical secretions that have physiological relevance (Rice and Cragg, 2008).
evidence: The results section compares DopaFilm sensitivity to receptor affinities with citation.

claim: SNRs for DopaFilm imaging were in the range of 5–50 for most experiments.
source: The optimizations in the NIR and SWIR regions facilitated imaging and recording of activity with exceedingly high signal-to-noise (SNR) ratios, attaining SNRs in the range of 5–50 for most experiments.
evidence: The results section describes imaging performance.

claim: The SNR for most TTX-free, optical stimulus-evoked release in axons frequently exceeded 30.
source: Incidentally, the SNR for most of our TTX-free, optical stimulus-evoked release in axons frequently exceeded 30 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative SNR measurements.
